title: the mudras
hook: a potter's hands, a cook's, a shopkeeper's: no sacred shape among them, and the Gita puts hands everywhere
tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)

segments.voice: Yesterday the mudras went on stage: where the hand goes, the eyes follow. Today, the last of the mudras, and the widest view of the hand.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `WHERE THE HAND GOES, THE EYES FOLLOW.`

segments.voice: A potter's wheel turns in a narrow lane. Two wet hands close around a lump of clay, and it rises into a wall, then a lip, then a bowl. Next door, a woman's hands press dough flat and slap it onto a hot pan. Across the lane, a shopkeeper counts out change. Nobody here is holding a sacred shape. All week the mudras have been hands that mean something on purpose. Today the Gita puts hands everywhere.
screen: `A POTTER'S HANDS. A COOK'S. A SHOPKEEPER'S.` → `NO SACRED SHAPE.` → `HANDS EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: In the thirteenth chapter of the Gita, Krishna describes what is to be known, the one reality behind everything, and the description begins with hands. In paraphrase: its hands and feet are everywhere; its eyes, heads and faces are everywhere; its ears are everywhere; it stands in the world, enfolding all. The Shvetashvatara Upanishad carries the same line, almost word for word. Then the next verse turns it around, in paraphrase: it shines through the workings of all the senses, and yet it is without senses; unattached, and yet it holds everything up. Hands everywhere, and no hands at all. Some commentators say it is spoken of as having hands because of the hands of all beings, through which it works, while it is never bound to any one of them. Some devotees hear something closer to home: the divine at work in every pair of hands. The verse leaves room for both. Now look back at the week of hands. A seal, pressed in so it holds. Anjali, the joined palms, a bow to you. Chin mudra, the small self bending to the great, under a banyan tree. The breathing hand at the nose. Abhaya and varada: do not fear, and give. The dancer's hand, with the eyes and mind following. Each was a hand shaped to carry a meaning. The Gita's line doesn't cancel any of that. It widens it: the hand before a shrine and the hand at the wheel or the stove, named in one breath. Some readers take the verse to say that every hand at work is already held inside a larger one.
screen: `GITA 13: HANDS AND FEET EVERYWHERE.` · `THE NEXT VERSE: AND WITHOUT SENSES.` · `THE WEEK OF SHAPED HANDS.` · `THE SHRINE AND THE STOVE, IN ONE BREATH.` · then, large: `HANDS EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Rest the hands on the thighs, palms up, and look at them: the lines, the knuckles, the places that do the work. Close the eyes and let other hands from your day come and go, the ones that grew and cooked your food, the ones that built your chair. Then settle back into your own open palms; if you pray, let the verse rest there, and if not, stay with their warmth and the breath.
The mudras. Today, the widest: what is to be known has hands and feet everywhere, and yet no senses.
Your line: hands and feet everywhere. Tomorrow the hands rest, and the mouth begins. That's day one thousand thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Hindus hold shaped hands in worship, practice and dance; some also reflect on Bhagavad Gita 13 and the Shvetashvatara Upanishad, which describe the one reality as having hands and feet everywhere.

fork.setup: you're watching a potter's hands shape a bowl. the Gita says what is to be known has hands everywhere. how do readers take it?
options: only the hands on temple images count.
it works through every pair of hands, and yet is never bound to any.

fork.reveal: Gita 13 gives it hands everywhere, and the next verse says it is without senses. some commentators read it as working through the hands of all beings; some devotees hear the divine at work in every pair of hands.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sarvatah-pani-padam, hands and feet everywhere, from Gita 13 and the Shvetashvatara Upanishad.

what it means: the week's shaped hands sit inside the Gita's wider line, hands everywhere.
what a scholar hears: sarvatah-pani-padam tat, Gita 13.13 and Shvetashvatara 3.16, balanced by sarvendriya-vivarjitam, without senses, in the next verse.

chat.says: What does the Gita mean when it says hands and feet everywhere?
options: Some read it as all beings' hands at work, yet the next verse says no senses.
It means only holy people's hands are divine, not ordinary workers'.
It's a poem describing a temple dancer's hand gestures.
chat.meaning: Gita 13 says what is to be known has hands and feet everywhere; the next verse adds that it is without senses, unattached.
